--- ## title: "Converted Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: default pagetitle: 'Multinomial $N$-mixture models' slide-number: true echo: true lang: en --- ## {content-align="center" style="font-size: 140%;"}
Lecture 7 -- Multinomial $N$-mixture models:
simulation, fitting, and prediction
::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} WILD(FISH) 8390
Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics :::
# Overview {visibility="hidden"} ## Overview ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} The objectives are the same as with binomial $N$-mixture models. - Estimate abundance - Model spatial variation in abundance/density ::: {.fragment} The difference is that, instead of repeated count data at each site, we have data from sampling methods such as: - Double observer sampling - Removal sampling - Mark-recapture - Distance sampling - And other methods that yield multinomial counts\dots ::: ::: ## Multinomial $N$-mixture model ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} State model (with Poisson assumption) $$ \mathrm{log}(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 {\color{blue} x_{i1}} + \beta_2 {\color{blue} x_{i2}} + \cdots \\ N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i) $$ Observation model $$ \mathrm{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 {\color{blue} x_{i1}} + \alpha_2 {\color{Purple} w_{ij}} + \cdots \\ \{y_{i1}, \dots, y_{iK}\} \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(N_i, \pi(p_{i1}, \dots, p_{iJ})) $$ Definitions ::: ::: {style='font-size: 60%;'} $\lambda_i$ -- Expected value of abundance at site $i$
$N_i$ -- Realized value of abundance at site $i$
$p_{ij}$ -- Probability of detecting *an individual* at site $i$ on occasion $j$
$\pi(p)$ -- Function mapping $J$ detection probs to $K$ multinomial cell probs
$y_{ik}$ -- Multinomial count data (*The final count is not observed!*)
$\color{blue} x_1$ and $\color{blue} x_2$ -- site covariates $\color{Purple} w$ -- observation covariate ::: ## The multinomial distribution ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} This is the first multivariate distribution we've covered. $$ \{y_{1}, \dots, y_{K}\} \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(N, \{\pi_i, \dots, \pi_K\}) $$ The multinomial describes how $N$ objects are distributed among $K$ classes (also called bins, categories, etc\dots). :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {style='font-size: 65%;'} Imagine $N=20$ animals are studied for 1 year and there are 3 possible "fates" with associated probabilities: $\Pr(\mathrm{survived})=0.5$, $\Pr(\mathrm{depredated})=0.3$, $\Pr(\mathrm{starved})=0.2$. Here is one possible outcome: ::: ::: {style='font-size: 85%;'} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} N <- 20 pi <- c(survived=0.5, depredated=0.3, starved=0.2) ## Probs must sum to 1 t(rmultinom(n=1, size=N, prob=pi)) ## Counts must sum to N ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` survived depredated starved [1,] 11 5 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Sampling methods ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} Benefits of the multinomial $N$-mixture model - Precision is typically better than binomial $N$-mixture models because there's more information in the data. - Can be applied to data from many sampling designs, simply by changing how the $\pi$ probabilities are computed. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {style='font-size: 65%;'} Removal sampling $$ {\pi(p)} = \{p, (1-p)p, (1-p)^2p, \dots, (1-p)^{K-1}p, (1-p)^K\} $$ Double observer (*independent observers*) $$ {\pi(p)} = \{p_1(1-p_2), (1-p_1)p_2, p_1p_2, (1-p_1)(1-p_2)\} $$ Double observer (*dependent observers*) $$ {\pi(p)} = \{p_1, (1-p_1)p_2, (1-p_1)(1-p_2)\} $$ ::: ::: # Removal sampling ## Removal sampling ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} Removal sampling is often used in electrofishing studies. A stream section is surveyed $J$ times, fish are removed on each "pass", and the rate of removal tells us about capture probability. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} - $y_{ij}$ -- number of individuals removed at site $i$ on pass $j$ - $p$ -- probability of catching an individual on a single pass ::: ::: {style='font-size: 60%;'} Description | Multinomial cell probability ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------ Pr(first captured on first pass) | $\pi_1 = p$ Pr(first captured on second pass) | $\pi_2 = (1-p)p$ Pr(first captured on third pass) | $\pi_3 = (1-p)(1-p)p$ $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ Pr(first captured on pass $J$) | $\pi_J = (1-p)^{J-1}p$ Pr(not captured) | $\pi_{J+1} = (1-p)^J$ ::: ::: ## [Simulating removal data, no covariates]{style="font-size: 90%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Abundance ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nSites <- 100 lambda1 <- 4.6 ## Expected value of N N1 <- rpois(n=nSites, lambda=lambda1) ``` ::: Capture probability and multinomial counts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nPasses <- 3 K <- nPasses+1 # multinomial cells p1 <- 0.4 pi1 <- c(p1, (1-p1)*p1, (1-p1)*(1-p1)*p1, (1-p1)^3) y1.all <- matrix(NA, nrow=nSites, ncol=K) for(i in 1:nSites) { y1.all[i,] <- rmultinom(n=1, size=N1[i], prob=pi1) } ``` ::: Discard final column of individuals not detected ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y1 <- y1.all[,-K] head(y1, n=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 0 1 1 [2,] 1 2 0 [3,] 2 0 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Simulated removal data ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} ::: {#tbl-kable .cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Pass 1 Pass 2 Pass 3
Site 1 0 1 1
Site 2 1 2 0
Site 3 2 0 1
Site 4 2 0 0
Site 5 7 1 1
Site 6 2 1 0
Site 7 3 2 1
Site 8 2 0 0
Site 9 4 0 1
Site 10 0 1 0
````` ::: ::: ::: ## Removal model, covariates ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Covariates ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} streamDepth <- rnorm(nSites) ``` ::: Coefficients, $\lambda$, and $p$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} beta0 <- 1; beta1 <- 0.5 lambda2 <- exp(beta0 + beta1*streamDepth) alpha0 <- 0; alpha1 <- -1 p2 <- plogis(alpha0 + alpha1*streamDepth) ``` ::: Simulate abundance and removal data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} N2 <- rpois(nSites, lambda=lambda2) ## local abundance y2.all <- pi2 <- matrix(NA, nrow=nSites, ncol=K) for(i in 1:nSites) { pi2[i,] <- c(p2[i], (1-p2[i])*p2[i], (1-p2[i])^2*p2[i], (1-p2[i])^3) y2.all[i,] <- rmultinom(n=1, size=N2[i], prob=pi2[i,]) } y2 <- y2.all[,-K] ## Discard final column... individuals not detected ``` ::: ::: ## Simulated data ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} Observations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y2[1:19,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 0 0 [2,] 0 0 0 [3,] 1 0 0 [4,] 1 1 0 [5,] 0 0 0 [6,] 0 0 0 [7,] 0 1 0 [8,] 1 0 0 [9,] 1 2 0 [10,] 2 0 0 [11,] 3 0 0 [12,] 2 0 0 [13,] 1 2 0 [14,] 0 0 0 [15,] 3 2 1 [16,] 0 0 0 [17,] 0 1 0 [18,] 4 1 1 [19,] 1 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'}
Summary stats
Captures on each pass ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} colSums(y2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 119 62 36 ``` ::: ::: Naive abundance ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(y2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 217 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Prepare data in 'unmarked' ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} umf <- unmarkedFrameMPois(y=y2, siteCovs=data.frame(streamDepth), type="removal") summary(umf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` unmarkedFrame Object 100 sites Maximum number of observations per site: 3 Mean number of observations per site: 3 Sites with at least one detection: 89 Tabulation of y observations: 0 1 2 3 4 153 98 32 13 4 Site-level covariates: streamDepth Min. :-2.328970 1st Qu.:-0.954293 Median : 0.001277 Mean :-0.120420 3rd Qu.: 0.569628 Max. : 2.610328 ``` ::: ::: ## Fit the model ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} `multinomPois` has similar arguments as `occu` and `pcount`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fm <- multinomPois(~streamDepth ~streamDepth, umf) fm ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: multinomPois(formula = ~streamDepth ~ streamDepth, data = umf) Abundance (log-scale): Estimate SE z P(>|z|) (Intercept) 1.04 0.101 10.31 6.29e-25 streamDepth 0.56 0.115 4.89 1.02e-06 Detection (logit-scale): Estimate SE z P(>|z|) (Intercept) -0.0426 0.214 -0.199 8.42e-01 streamDepth -1.0084 0.171 -5.902 3.59e-09 AIC: 603.3294 Number of sites: 100 ``` ::: ::: Compare to actual parameter values: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(beta0=beta0, beta1=beta1); c(alpha0=alpha0, alpha1=alpha1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` beta0 beta1 1.0 0.5 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` alpha0 alpha1 0 -1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## [Empirical Bayes -- Site-level abundance]{style="font-size: 90%;"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} re <- ranef(fm, K=15) plot(re, layout=c(4,3), subset=site%in%1:12, xlim=c(-1, 11), lwd=5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-Nmix-multinomial-I_files/figure-revealjs/ranef-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Total abundance (in surveyed region) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} N.total.post <- predict(re, func=sum, nsim=1000) hist(N.total.post, freq=FALSE, main="", xlab="N total", ylab="Probability") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-Nmix-multinomial-I_files/figure-revealjs/Ntotal-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Prediction in 'unmarked' Create `data.frame` with prediction covariates. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pred.data <- data.frame(streamDepth=seq(-3, 3, length=20)) ``` ::: Get predictions of $\lambda$ for each row of prediction data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lambda.pred <- predict(fm, newdata=pred.data, type='state', append=TRUE) ``` ::: View $\lambda$ predictions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(head(lambda.pred), digits=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Predicted SE lower upper streamDepth 1 0.53 0.16 0.29 0.97 -3.0 2 0.63 0.17 0.37 1.08 -2.7 3 0.75 0.18 0.47 1.20 -2.4 4 0.90 0.19 0.60 1.35 -2.1 5 1.07 0.19 0.76 1.51 -1.7 6 1.28 0.18 0.97 1.70 -1.4 ``` ::: ::: ## Prediction in 'unmarked' ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(Predicted ~ streamDepth, lambda.pred, ylab="Expected value of abundance", ylim=c(0,20), xlab="Stream depth", type="l", lwd=2) lines(lower ~ streamDepth, lambda.pred, col="grey") lines(upper ~ streamDepth, lambda.pred, col="grey") points(rowSums(y2)~streamDepth) lines(lowess(rowSums(y2)~streamDepth), col="blue", lwd=2) ## Lowess line for fun (it's way off) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-Nmix-multinomial-I_files/figure-revealjs/pred-lam2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## [Bayesian multinomial *N*-mixture models]{style="font-size: 90%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} There are several equivalent formulations of the multinomial that can be used to fit the model. - Conditional-on-$N$, missing $y_{iK}$ (Not possible in JAGS) - Conditional-on-$N$, conditional on $n_i=\sum_{k=1}^{K-1} y_{i,k}$ - Conditional-on-$N$, sequential binomial - Marginalized $N$ These are just probability tricks that can affect MCMC performance. See AHM I for details. Here, we will focus on the second option. ::: ## Conditional-on-*N* and *n~i~* ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} We can break the problem down into two steps by conditioning on $n_i$, the number of individuals captured at site $i$: $$ n_i \sim \mathrm{Bin}(N_i, 1-\pi_K) \\ \{y_{i,1}, \dots, y_{i,K-1}\} \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(n_i, \{\pi_{i,1}, \dots, \pi_{i,K-1}\}/(1-\pi_K)) $$ Note that the modified cell probabilities still sum to 1. ::: ## Conditional-on-*N* and *n~i~* [removal-mod2.jag](removal-mod2.jag) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { lambda.intercept ~ dunif(0, 5) beta0 <- log(lambda.intercept) beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) alpha0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) alpha1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) for(i in 1:nSites) { log(lambda[i]) <- beta0 + beta1*streamDepth[i] N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i]) # Latent local abundance logit(p[i]) <- alpha0 + alpha1*streamDepth[i] pi[i,1] <- p[i] ## Pr(first captured in first pass) pi[i,2] <- (1-p[i])*p[i] ## Pr(first captured in second pass) pi[i,3] <- (1-p[i])^2*p[i] ## Pr(first captured in third pass) pi[i,4] <- (1-p[i])^3 ## Pr(not captured) n[i] ~ dbin(1-pi[i,4], N[i]) ## nCaptured at site i y[i,1:3] ~ dmulti(pi[i,1:3]/(1-pi[i,4]), n[i]) } totalAbundance <- sum(N[1:nSites]) } ``` ::: ::: ## Data, inits, and parameters Put data in a named list ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.data.rem2 <- list(y=y2, n=rowSums(y2), streamDepth=streamDepth, nSites=nSites, nPasses=nPasses) ``` ::: Initial values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.inits.rem <- function() { list(lambda.intercept=runif(1), alpha0=rnorm(1), N=rowSums(y2)+rpois(nrow(y2), 2)) } ``` ::: Parameters to monitor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.pars.rem <- c("beta0", "beta1", "alpha0", "alpha1", "totalAbundance") ``` ::: ## MCMC ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(jagsUI); library(coda) jags.post.rem2 <- jags.basic(data=jags.data.rem2, inits=jags.inits.rem, parameters.to.save=jags.pars.rem, model.file="removal-mod2.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(jags.post.rem2[,jags.pars.rem]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Iterations = 101:2100 Thinning interval = 1 Number of chains = 3 Sample size per chain = 2000 1. Empirical mean and standard deviation for each variable, plus standard error of the mean: Mean SD Naive SE Time-series SE beta0 1.06570 0.1093 0.001411 0.007564 beta1 0.57281 0.1261 0.001628 0.011016 alpha0 -0.07862 0.2253 0.002908 0.013519 alpha1 -1.01330 0.1841 0.002376 0.012184 totalAbundance 340.36600 63.0831 0.814399 6.550871 2. Quantiles for each variable: 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% beta0 0.8659 0.9922 1.05966 1.13139 1.3061 beta1 0.3523 0.4869 0.56798 0.64469 0.8707 alpha0 -0.5743 -0.2215 -0.06564 0.07506 0.3392 alpha1 -1.3958 -1.1346 -1.01035 -0.89113 -0.6677 totalAbundance 262.0000 300.0000 328.00000 363.00000 519.0000 ``` ::: ::: ## Traceplots and density plots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(jags.post.rem2[,jags.pars.rem[1:3]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-Nmix-multinomial-I_files/figure-revealjs/bugs-plot1-rem2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=0.7
textwidth} ::: ::: ## Traceplots and density plots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(jags.post.rem2[,jags.pars.rem[4:5]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-Nmix-multinomial-I_files/figure-revealjs/bugs-plot2-rem2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=0.7
textwidth} ::: ::: ## Convergence diagnostics Gelman-Rubin diagnostic ($\hat{R}$) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gelman.diag(jags.post.rem2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Potential scale reduction factors: Point est. Upper C.I. alpha0 1.04 1.13 alpha1 1.06 1.18 beta0 1.05 1.15 beta1 1.08 1.24 totalAbundance 1.11 1.32 Multivariate psrf 1.06 ``` ::: ::: Convergence is suggested by $\hat{R}$ close to 1. ## Effective posterior sample size It's a good idea to have >500 effective posterior samples. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame(ESS = effectiveSize(jags.post.rem2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ESS alpha0 307.4293 alpha1 305.4935 beta0 253.1546 beta1 169.4270 totalAbundance 111.7783 ``` ::: ::: ## Closing thoughts on removal models ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} In addition to site covariates, you could also include observation covariates, but it's hard to think of realistic covariates that would be specific to each pass.
::: {.fragment} Removal models get used in many scenarios other than electrofishing: - Point count surveys * Observers keep track of individuals during the survey * Analyze number of new individuals detected during each time interval ::: ::: {.fragment} - Mark-recapture surveys * If behavior responses (trap shyness or trap happiness) are extreme, recaptures can be discarded and removal models can be applied. ::: ::: # Double observer sampling ## [Double observer sampling (independent)]{style="font-size: 85%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 65%;'} Two observers sample the same location at the same time, working independently. After each survey, they compare notes and figure out which individual were detected by observer A only, B only, or by both. ::: {.fragment} - $y_{i1}$ -- number of individuals detected only by observer A - $y_{i2}$ -- number of individuals detected only by observer B - $y_{i3}$ -- number of individuals detected by observers A and B - $p_1$ -- probability that observer A detects an individual - $p_2$ -- probability that observer B detects an individual Description | Multinomial cell probability -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ Pr(detected by observer A but not B) | $\pi_1 = p_1(1-p_2)$ Pr(detected by observer B but not A) | $\pi_2 = (1-p_1)p_2$ Pr(detected by observers A and B) | $\pi_3 = p_1p_2$ Pr(not detected) | $\pi_4 = (1-p_1)(1-p_2)$ ::: ::: ## [Double observer sampling (dependent)]{style="font-size: 85%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 65%;'} Two observers sample at the same time, but observer B only records what observer A missed. Often used in aerial waterfowl surveys.
Observers should switch roles to ensure parameter identifiability.
::: {.fragment} - $y_{i1}$ -- number of individuals detected by observer A - $y_{i2}$ -- number of individuals missed by A but detected by B - $p_1$ -- probability that observer A detects an individual - $p_2$ -- probability that observer B detects an individual Description | Multinomial cell probability -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ Pr(detected by observer A) | $\pi_1 = p_1$ Pr(detected by observer B but not A) | $\pi_2 = (1-p_1)p_2$ Pr(not detected) | $\pi_3 = (1-p_1)(1-p_2)$ ::: ::: ## [Simulating dependent double observer data]{style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Abundance ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nSites <- 100 lambda <- 4.6 # Expected value of N N <- rpois(n=nSites, lambda=lambda) ``` ::: Detection probability and multinomial counts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} observer <- matrix(c("A","B","B","A"), nrow=nSites, ncol=2, byrow=TRUE) p1 <- 0.4 # Detection prob for observer A p2 <- 0.3 # Detection prob for observer B piAfirst <- c(p1, (1-p1)*p2, (1-p1)*(1-p2)) piBfirst <- c(p2, (1-p2)*p1, (1-p1)*(1-p2)) K <- length(piAfirst) y.all <- matrix(NA, nrow=nSites, ncol=K) for(i in 1:nSites) { pi <- if(observer[i,1]=="A") piAfirst else piBfirst y.all[i,] <- rmultinom(n=1, size=N[i], prob=pi) } ``` ::: Discard final column of individuals not detected ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- y.all[,-K] ``` ::: ::: ## [Dependent double observer model in JAGS]{style="font-size: 85%;"} [double-obs-dep.jag](double-obs-dep.jag) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { lambda ~ dunif(0, 20) # Prior on E(N) p1 ~ dunif(0, 1) # Prior on observer A detection prob p2 ~ dunif(0, 1) # Prior on observer B detection prob # Multinomial cell probs piAfirst <- c(p1, (1-p1)*p2, (1-p1)*(1-p2)) # When obs A goes first piBfirst <- c(p2, (1-p2)*p1, (1-p1)*(1-p2)) # When obs B goes first for(i in 1:nSites) { N[i] ~ dpois(lambda) # Latent local abundance pi[i,1:3] <- ifelse(observer[i,1]==1, piAfirst, piBfirst) n[i] ~ dbin(1-pi[i,3], N[i]) ## nDetected at site i y[i,1:2] ~ dmulti(pi[i,1:2]/(1-pi[i,3]), n[i]) } totalAbundance <- sum(N[1:nSites]) } ``` ::: ::: ## Data, inits, and parameters Put data in a named list ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.data.double <- list(y=y, n=rowSums(y), nSites=nSites, observer=ifelse(observer=="A", 1, 2)) ``` ::: Initial values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.inits.doub <- function() { list(lambda=runif(1), p1=runif(1), p2=runif(1), N=rowSums(y)+rpois(nrow(y), 2)) } ``` ::: Parameters to monitor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.pars.doub <- c("lambda", "p1", "p2", "totalAbundance") ``` ::: ## MCMC ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.post.doub <- jags.basic(data=jags.data.double, inits=jags.inits.doub, parameters.to.save=jags.pars.doub, model.file="double-obs-dep.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(summary(jags.post.doub)$quantiles, digits=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% lambda 3.141 3.587 3.891 4.322 5.577 p1 0.299 0.409 0.467 0.519 0.608 p2 0.238 0.334 0.383 0.427 0.511 totalAbundance 321.975 359.000 387.000 428.000 556.025 ``` ::: ::: ## [Additional remarks on double observer models]{style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} ::: {.fragment .semi-fade-out fragment-index=1} In practice, there are often many observers on a project, even though only two survey at a time. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out .semi-fade-out fragment-index=1} We can deal with this by including "observer ID" as an observation covariate. Everything else stays the same. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out .semi-fade-out fragment-index=2} It can be hard to pull of the independent double observer method because observers often influence each other while working. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out .semi-fade-out fragment-index=3} All of these methods require some sort of *short-term* individual identification of animals, even though they aren't being marked. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out .semi-fade-out fragment-index=4} If short-term individual ID isn't possible, you could fall back on binomial $N$-mixture models. ::: ::: # Assignment ## Assignment ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} Create a self-contained R script or Rmarkdown file to do the following: - Simulate *independent* double observer data with the following properties: * nSites=200 * $\lambda=3$ * $p_1=0.3$ and $p_2=0.5$ - Fit the model using 'unmarked.' You will need to create an observation covariate indicating observer A and B. When you create the `unmarkedFrameMPois`, use `type="double"`. - Fit the same model in JAGS - For both unmarked and JAGS, use the point estimates of $p_1$ and $p_2$ to compute the $\pi$ probabilities.
Upload your `.R`, `.Rmd`, or `.qmd` file to ELC by 5:00pm on Tuesday.
:::

        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
